Features: (1) popular sovereignty - ultimate power belongs to the people; (2) free, fair and regular elections with universal adult franchise; (3) political equality ('one person, one vote, one value'); (4) majority rule with protection of minority rights; (5) rule of law and constitutionalism; (6) protection of fundamental rights and civil liberties - especially freedom of speech, press, assembly and association; (7) an independent judiciary; (8) accountability and responsibility of government; (9) multi-party system and a strong opposition; (10) separation or distribution of powers; (11) free press and media; and (12) peaceful transfer of power.

Robert Dahl's criteria for democracy include effective participation, voting equality, enlightened understanding, control of the agenda and inclusion of adults. International indices (Freedom House, V-Dem, the Economist Intelligence Unit's Democracy Index) measure democracy using such features.
Direct democracy allows citizens themselves to decide public questions rather than acting only through representatives.

In direct democracy, citizens participate personally in making laws and decisions. Ancient Athens (fifth century BCE) is the classic example: the Ecclesia (Assembly) of adult male citizens met about 40 times a year; the Boule (Council of 500) was chosen by lot; and juries were chosen by lot. Women, slaves and foreigners were excluded. Rousseau favoured direct democracy, saying sovereignty cannot be represented.

Modern forms include the Swiss Landsgemeinde (in Appenzell Innerrhoden and Glarus), New England town meetings, the gram sabha in Indian villages (Article 243A), and devices of direct democracy - referendum, initiative, recall and plebiscite - used in Switzerland, US states, Italy and elsewhere. Direct democracy encourages participation and legitimacy but is difficult in large, complex societies; digital tools have opened new possibilities ('e-democracy').
Indirect or representative democracy allows citizens to elect representatives who make decisions and laws on their behalf.

In indirect (representative) democracy, people elect representatives to make laws and govern for a fixed period. It is necessary in large states such as India (the world's largest democracy, with about 97 crore registered voters in 2024). Representatives are accountable through periodic elections, and the legislature controls the executive.

Forms: parliamentary (India, UK, Japan) and presidential (USA, Brazil); electoral systems include first-past-the-post, proportional representation, mixed systems (Germany) and the single transferable vote. Merits: practicality, decision-making by informed representatives, stability and protection of minorities through institutions. Demerits: citizens participate mainly during elections; representatives may ignore voters; parties and money influence elections. Participatory and deliberative democracy aim to increase citizen involvement between elections.
Procedural democracy focuses on institutions and procedures such as competitive elections, voting and rules for forming governments.

Procedural democracy is a 'minimal' definition that focuses on the rules and procedures for selecting governments: regular, free and fair elections; universal adult suffrage; competition among multiple parties; freedom to campaign; secret ballot; and peaceful transfer of power. Joseph Schumpeter ('Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy', 1942) and Samuel Huntington ('The Third Wave', 1991) used procedural definitions: a country is democratic if its most powerful decision-makers are selected through fair, honest and periodic elections in which candidates freely compete and virtually all adults can vote.

Advantages: it is clear and measurable, and it allows comparison between countries. Limitations: a country may hold elections but still suffer from inequality, discrimination, restrictions on rights or manipulation of institutions - sometimes called 'electoral democracy' or 'illiberal democracy' (Fareed Zakaria, 1997).
Substantive democracy asks whether democratic government also produces meaningful equality, rights, participation and social justice.

Substantive democracy (or 'thick' or 'maximal' democracy) asks whether democracy delivers real outcomes for citizens: protection of civil liberties and minority rights, social and economic equality, social justice, gender equality, dignity and meaningful participation of all groups, including the poor and marginalised. It is concerned with the quality of democracy, not only its procedures.

Thinkers such as Ambedkar (who stressed social democracy based on liberty, equality and fraternity), C. B. Macpherson, Amartya Sen (democracy as public reasoning and expanding capabilities) and supporters of participatory democracy emphasise substantive democracy. In India, the Directive Principles, reservations, welfare schemes and social justice movements aim at substantive democracy. Both procedural and substantive aspects are necessary: procedures without substance can become hollow, while substance without procedures can lead to authoritarianism.
Challenges may include corruption, inequality, political violence, weak participation, misinformation and misuse of power.

Challenges to democracy in general include: economic inequality and poverty; corruption; criminalisation of politics (in 2024, a large share of elected Lok Sabha members faced criminal cases, according to the Association for Democratic Reforms); money power in elections; communalism and casteism; regionalism and separatism; political violence; low participation of women and marginalised groups; illiteracy and lack of political awareness; decline of internal democracy in parties and dynastic politics; misuse of power and weakening of institutions; misinformation and fake news on social media; polarisation; populism; and threats to press freedom and civil liberties.

Global trends include 'democratic backsliding' (V-Dem reports describe 'electoral autocracies'), the rise of authoritarian populism, foreign interference in elections and the influence of technology companies. In India, specific concerns include delays in justice, pressure on the media and civil society, and the misuse of investigative agencies, while defenders point to the strength of Indian elections and institutions.
Possible remedies include stronger institutions, transparency, civic education, accountability, free and fair elections and protection of rights.

Remedies: (1) electoral reforms - state funding of elections, transparency in political funding (the Supreme Court struck down the electoral bond scheme in 2024), limits on expenditure, decriminalisation (disclosure of criminal records, fast-track courts for politicians), and strengthening the Election Commission's independence; (2) strengthening institutions - an independent judiciary, Lokpal (2013 Act) and Lokayuktas against corruption, CAG, CVC and the Right to Information Act (2005); (3) inner-party democracy and regulation of parties; (4) decentralisation - empowering panchayats and municipalities; (5) civic and political education, media literacy and an informed citizenry; (6) protection of rights and freedom of the press; (7) inclusion of women and marginalised groups (reservations, women's reservation 2023); (8) reducing poverty and inequality; and (9) combating misinformation while protecting free speech.

Ultimately, democracy depends on active citizenship - people voting, participating, questioning and holding governments accountable. As Jawaharlal Nehru said, democracy requires discipline, tolerance and mutual regard.
The Election Commission of India is a constitutional body responsible for the superintendence, direction and control of specified elections.

Article 324 of the Constitution vests the superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President in the Election Commission. It was established on 25 January 1950, celebrated as National Voters' Day since 2011. Sukumar Sen was the first Chief Election Commissioner, conducting the first general elections in 1951-1952, which involved about 17 crore voters.

The ECI is a permanent and independent constitutional body. Elections to panchayats and municipalities are conducted by State Election Commissions (Articles 243K and 243ZA). Related laws include the Representation of the People Acts of 1950 (electoral rolls, delimitation) and 1951 (conduct of elections, qualifications and disqualifications, electoral offences, disputes).
The Election Commission consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and such number of other Election Commissioners as provided under the constitutional and legal framework.

Article 324(2) provides that the ECI shall consist of the Chief Election Commissioner and such number of other Election Commissioners as the President may fix. Until 1989, it was a single-member body. Two additional commissioners were appointed in October 1989 but the posts were abolished in January 1990; since October 1993, the ECI has been a three-member body (the CEC and two ECs), with decisions taken by majority. The Supreme Court upheld this in T. N. Seshan v. Union of India (1995).

Appointment: by the President. The Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, provides for a selection committee of the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM (earlier, in Anoop Baranwal, 2023, the Supreme Court had said the CJI should be included until Parliament made a law). Term: six years or until the age of 65. Removal: the CEC can be removed only in the manner and on the grounds of a Supreme Court judge (special majority of Parliament); the ECs can be removed by the President on the recommendation of the CEC. The independence of appointments remains debated.
Its functions include supervising elections, electoral administration and ensuring that elections are conducted according to constitutional and legal requirements.

Functions: (1) preparing and updating electoral rolls and registering voters (with Electors Photo Identity Cards, introduced in 1993); (2) delimitation-related functions (delimitation itself is done by the Delimitation Commission); (3) notifying election schedules; (4) recognising political parties as national or state parties and allotting symbols (the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968), and deciding disputes over symbols; (5) scrutiny of nominations; (6) enforcing the Model Code of Conduct (developed from 1960 in Kerala and adopted nationally, it applies from the announcement of elections); (7) monitoring election expenditure; (8) appointing observers; (9) conducting polls using EVMs and VVPATs; (10) counting votes and declaring results; and (11) advising the President and Governors on disqualification of members (Articles 103 and 192).

It also conducts voter awareness through SVEEP (Systematic Voters' Education and Electoral Participation), introduced NOTA (after the Supreme Court's PUCL judgement, 2013), and ensures accessibility for persons with disabilities and elderly voters (home voting). It can postpone or cancel elections in case of malpractices.
By administering elections and protecting electoral integrity, the ECI performs an important role in India's representative democracy.

The ECI is considered a guardian of democracy because it has conducted free and fair elections in a vast, diverse country - from the 1951-1952 elections to the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, with about 64 crore votes cast - ensuring peaceful transfers of power. T. N. Seshan (CEC 1990-1996) transformed the ECI by strictly enforcing the Model Code of Conduct, curbing election expenditure and malpractices, and introducing voter ID cards. J. M. Lyngdoh and others continued reforms.

Innovations include EVMs (used in all constituencies since 2004), VVPAT (from 2013, made universal in 2019), facilities for voters with disabilities, the cVIGIL app for reporting violations, and webcasting of polling stations. Challenges and criticisms: allegations of partiality in enforcing the Model Code, questions about the independence of appointments, concerns about EVMs (rejected by the Supreme Court in 2024, which upheld the EVM-VVPAT system), money power, hate speech, paid news and misinformation. Maintaining public trust in the ECI is essential for Indian democracy.

sections.title: Meaning, Features and Forms of Democracy

blocks.text:
Democracy is based on the principle that political authority belongs to the people. Its major features include participation, political equality, regular elections, accountability, rights and rule of law.

Direct democracy permits citizens to decide issues themselves. Indirect or representative democracy works through elected representatives. Large modern states mainly depend on representative institutions.

Democracy therefore concerns both popular authority and the institutional arrangements through which that authority is exercised.

Meaning: democracy means rule by the people, based on popular sovereignty and consent. Definitions by Lincoln, Schumpeter, Dahl and Ambedkar emphasise popular authority, competitive elections, participation and peaceful social transformation. Democracy can be seen as a form of government, a form of state, a social order and a way of life.

Features: free and fair elections with universal adult franchise; political equality; majority rule and minority rights; rule of law; fundamental rights and civil liberties; independent judiciary; accountability; free press; multi-party competition; and peaceful transfer of power. Forms: direct democracy (Athens, Swiss cantons, gram sabhas, referendum, initiative, recall) and indirect or representative democracy (parliamentary and presidential). Large modern states depend on representative democracy, sometimes combined with direct democratic devices and decentralisation.

Evaluation: merits - it respects human dignity, ensures accountability and responsiveness, protects rights, allows peaceful change, educates citizens and promotes legitimacy. Criticisms - it may be slow, costly, influenced by money and populism, and at risk of majority tyranny. Churchill's remark: 'Democracy is the worst form of government except for all those other forms that have been tried.' Democracy thus concerns both the principle of popular authority and the institutions through which it is exercised.

Procedural democracy focuses on democratic methods such as elections, voting, competition and constitutional procedures. A system may satisfy these requirements when governments are chosen through established democratic rules.

Substantive democracy goes further and asks whether people enjoy meaningful rights, equality, participation and social justice in practice.

The distinction is useful because elections are essential to democracy, but democratic quality also depends on how institutions affect citizens' actual lives.

Procedural democracy: focuses on institutions and procedures - competitive elections, universal suffrage, party competition, freedom of campaign, secret ballot and constitutional rules for forming and changing governments. Schumpeter's elite competition theory and Huntington's 'third wave' studies used procedural definitions. It is minimal and measurable but may treat countries as democratic even if they lack real freedoms or equality.

Substantive democracy: asks whether democracy secures civil liberties, rule of law, social and economic justice, equality of opportunity, gender equality, minority protection and meaningful participation. It reflects Ambedkar's idea that political democracy must rest on social democracy, and Sen's view of democracy as public reasoning and the expansion of freedoms. It is broader but harder to measure and may risk subjectivity about which outcomes count.

Relationship: elections are essential, but democratic quality also depends on how institutions affect people's lives. In India, procedural democracy is strong (regular elections, high turnout, peaceful transfers), while substantive democracy faces challenges (poverty, caste discrimination, gender inequality, communal tensions, access to justice). Both dimensions are needed; procedures provide the means and substance gives meaning to democracy.

Democratic systems may face corruption, inequality, misuse of public power, political violence, weak citizen participation and other problems. Such conditions can weaken public confidence and reduce meaningful democratic choice.

Remedies include stronger constitutional institutions, transparent administration, political accountability, civic education, protection of rights and genuinely free and fair elections.

Democracy must therefore be continuously protected through both institutions and active citizenship.

Challenges: socio-economic (poverty, inequality, unemployment, illiteracy), political (corruption, criminalisation, money power, defections, dynastic politics, lack of inner-party democracy, decline of parliamentary debate), social (communalism, casteism, regionalism, gender inequality), institutional (judicial delays, weakening of independent institutions, misuse of investigative agencies), and new threats (misinformation and fake news on social media, polarisation, populism, surveillance and threats to privacy). Political violence and insurgency in some regions also undermine democracy.

Remedies: electoral reforms (transparent funding, decriminalisation, independence of the ECI); anti-corruption institutions (Lokpal, RTI, whistle-blower protection); judicial reforms to reduce delays; strengthening of Parliament, opposition and committees; inner-party democracy; decentralisation through panchayats and municipalities; empowerment of women and marginalised groups; media freedom and fact-checking; civic education; inclusive economic development; and active civil society.

Conclusion: democracy is not self-sustaining; it must be protected through strong institutions, a culture of tolerance, rule of law and active, informed citizens. As Ambedkar warned, constitutional morality - respect for constitutional norms and methods - must be cultivated, and people must not lay their liberties at the feet of even a great leader ('bhakti' in politics leads to dictatorship).

sections.title: Election Commission of India and Indian Democracy

blocks.text:
The Election Commission of India is a constitutional body responsible for the superintendence, direction and control of elections within its constitutional mandate. It includes the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners as provided by law.

Its electoral functions are important because representative democracy requires credible elections. By administering the electoral process and seeking to maintain electoral integrity, the ECI acts as an important guardian of Indian democracy.

Constitutional position: Article 324 establishes the ECI as an independent body; Articles 325 (no one excluded from electoral rolls on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex), 326 (adult suffrage), 327-329 (laws on elections, bar on interference by courts in electoral matters except through election petitions). Composition: the CEC and two ECs; appointment under the 2023 Act; security of tenure for the CEC. Functions: electoral rolls, voter IDs, recognition of parties and symbols, Model Code of Conduct, election schedules, conduct of polls with EVMs and VVPAT, expenditure monitoring, observers, and advice on disqualifications.

Role as guardian: the ECI has conducted the world's largest elections, ensured peaceful transfers of power, increased participation (women's turnout now equals or exceeds men's in many states), and introduced reforms under leaders such as T. N. Seshan. It has acted against malpractices, booth capturing and misuse of official machinery. Challenges: money power, criminalisation, communal campaigning, social media misinformation, allegations of partisanship, questions about appointments, and voter roll issues.

Reforms suggested: a collegium-type appointment process for independence; constitutional protection for all Election Commissioners; powers to deregister parties; state funding of elections (Indrajit Gupta Committee, 1998); simultaneous elections (debated - 'One Nation, One Election' proposal, 2024); and stronger action on hate speech and paid news. A credible and impartial ECI is indispensable for representative democracy in India.
Plato connects justice with harmony. A just state exists when each class performs its proper function without interfering with the functions of others.

Plato (427-347 BCE), a disciple of Socrates and founder of the Academy in Athens, wrote 'The Republic' (subtitled 'Concerning Justice'), 'The Statesman' and 'The Laws'. In the Republic, he rejected popular views of justice: Cephalus (speaking the truth and paying debts), Polemarchus (doing good to friends and harm to enemies), Thrasymachus ('justice is the interest of the stronger') and Glaucon (justice as a convention born of fear).

Plato's own theory: justice is 'doing one's own work and not meddling with what is not one's own'. Corresponding to the three parts of the human soul - reason, spirit and appetite - there are three classes in the state: rulers (philosophers, with the virtue of wisdom), auxiliaries or warriors (courage) and producers (temperance). Justice is the harmony that results when each class performs its function under the guidance of reason. It is both individual (harmony of the soul) and social. Critics (Karl Popper, 'The Open Society and Its Enemies', 1945) called it totalitarian, as it subordinates the individual to the state and creates rigid classes.
Plato considers education essential for developing character and identifying people suitable for different social and political roles.

Plato considered education 'the one great thing'; Rousseau called the Republic 'the finest treatise on education ever written'. Education was a state responsibility, compulsory for both men and women, aimed at developing character and selecting rulers. The first stage (up to about 20 years) included music (literature, poetry, arts - censored to promote virtue) for the soul and gymnastics for the body.

Those who showed ability went on to higher education (20-30 years) in mathematics, geometry, astronomy and the sciences; the best studied dialectics (philosophy) from 30 to 35; then gained practical experience in administration for 15 years; and at 50, the philosopher-kings would rule, having attained knowledge of the 'Form of the Good'. Plato's theory emphasised equal education for women, merit and lifelong learning, but has been criticised for censorship and an elitist system.
Plato proposes communal arrangements for the guardian class to prevent private interests from corrupting political duty.

Plato's communism applied only to the ruling classes (guardians and auxiliaries), not to the producers. It had two parts: (1) communism of property - guardians would have no private property, live in common barracks, eat together and receive necessities from the producers, so they would not be corrupted by greed; and (2) communism of wives and children (abolition of the family) - marriages would be arranged by the state through festivals for eugenic purposes, children would be brought up in state nurseries without knowing their parents, so that guardians would regard all as one family and be free from selfish attachments.

Its purpose was political - to ensure that rulers devoted themselves fully to the public good and to unify the state - not economic equality. It differs from Marxian communism, which is economic, applies to all society and aims at abolition of classes. Aristotle criticised it: 'what is common to the greatest number has the least care bestowed upon it'; abolishing the family would weaken affection; and it ignores human nature.
Plato's ideal state is organised into classes and governed by philosopher-rulers possessing knowledge and virtue.

Plato's ideal state is described in the Republic. Its features: (1) rule by philosopher-kings - 'until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy... cities will never have rest from their evils'; (2) division of society into three functional classes based on aptitude (the 'myth of metals' - rulers of gold, auxiliaries of silver, producers of iron and bronze, with mobility based on merit); (3) justice as harmony; (4) state-controlled education; (5) communism of property and family for guardians; (6) equality of women, who could become guardians; and (7) the rule of reason rather than law.

Plato called it a 'pattern laid up in heaven'. In 'The Laws', written later, he proposed a 'second-best' state ruled by law, with private property and family. Criticisms: it is utopian, authoritarian, ignores individual freedom and consent, has no checks on rulers and treats producers as passive. Nevertheless, Plato raised fundamental questions about justice, education and the qualifications of rulers.
Aristotle classifies constitutions according to the number who rule and whether they govern for the common good or private interest.

Aristotle (384-322 BCE), Plato's student and tutor of Alexander the Great, founded the Lyceum. In 'Politics', he classified constitutions based on two criteria: (1) the number of rulers (one, few or many) and (2) the purpose of rule (the common good - 'true' or 'normal' forms; or the interest of the rulers - 'perverted' forms). True forms: monarchy (rule of one for all), aristocracy (rule of the virtuous few) and polity (rule of the many in the common interest). Perverted forms: tyranny (one for himself), oligarchy (the rich few for themselves) and democracy (the poor many for themselves).

He believed constitutions change in a cycle: monarchy degenerates into tyranny, which is replaced by aristocracy, which degenerates into oligarchy, followed by polity, which degenerates into democracy, and then back to monarchy. Aristotle based his classification on a study of 158 Greek constitutions, which shows his empirical method. Criticisms: the classification is based on Greek city-states, does not fit modern nation-states, and his use of 'democracy' as a perverted form differs from modern usage.
Aristotle favours a practical constitutional order based on moderation and a strong middle element rather than an unattainable ideal.

Aristotle distinguished the ideal state (best in theory) from the best practicable state (best for most states under normal conditions). The best practicable state is the 'polity', a mixed constitution combining elements of oligarchy (rule of the rich) and democracy (rule of the poor), based on the principle of the 'golden mean' (moderation, avoiding extremes). It is dominated by a large middle class, which is neither too rich (arrogant) nor too poor (envious), and therefore stable and fair.

Features include rule of law (law as 'reason unaffected by desire'), moderate property qualifications for citizenship, participation of citizens in deliberation and justice, and a balance of interests. Aristotle's ideal of the middle class and mixed constitution influenced later ideas of constitutional government, checks and balances (Polybius, Cicero, Montesquieu) and modern democracy.
Aristotle examines inequality, injustice and political conflict as causes of revolution and considers ways of preserving constitutions.

In Book V of 'Politics', Aristotle analysed revolutions (changes in constitution or rulers). General causes: the desire for equality (by the many, who feel unequally treated) and the desire for superiority (by the few who think they deserve more) - in short, disagreements about justice and inequality. Particular causes include insolence and greed of rulers, fear, contempt, disproportionate increase in some part of the state, election intrigues, neglect of small changes, dissimilarity of elements (different races), and foreign influence.

Ways to prevent revolution: maintaining the rule of law and respect for the constitution; preventing small violations; avoiding extremes of wealth and poverty and strengthening the middle class; educating citizens in the spirit of the constitution; short terms of office; not allowing anyone excessive power; honest administration; and giving offices based on merit. Aristotle also gave advice for preserving each type of constitution, and even described how tyrants maintain power. His analysis is considered one of the first systematic studies of political change.
Aristotle defended the controversial idea of natural slavery, a view rejected by modern principles of equality and human rights.

Aristotle argued that slavery is natural: some people are by nature fitted to rule (masters, who possess reason) and others to be ruled (slaves, who can understand reason but cannot use it to govern themselves). The slave is 'a living tool' or 'animate instrument' of the household, and slavery benefits both master and slave. He distinguished natural slavery from legal or conventional slavery (such as prisoners of war), which he considered unjust if the enslaved were naturally free, especially if Greeks were enslaved.

He recommended that masters treat slaves humanely and that slaves be allowed to earn freedom. His theory reflected the Greek economy, which depended on slave labour, and Greek prejudices against 'barbarians'. It was later used to justify slavery in the Americas. Modern ideas of human equality, dignity and human rights (UDHR Article 4: 'No one shall be held in slavery') completely reject it.
Machiavelli treats politics as having its own practical requirements and analyses religion and morality in relation to political stability and power.

Niccolò Machiavelli (1469-1527) was a Florentine diplomat and official. After the Medici returned to power (1512), he was dismissed, tortured and exiled to his farm, where he wrote 'The Prince' (1513, published 1532), dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici, and 'Discourses on the First Ten Books of Livy' (on republics). He is called the 'father of modern political science' and the first modern political thinker because he separated politics from ethics and religion.

He argued that the ruler must be ready to act immorally when necessary for the security of the state - 'a prince who wishes to maintain himself must learn how not to be good' - and that the end (preserving the state) justifies the means (a phrase associated with him, though not his exact words). The prince should be both a 'fox' (to recognise traps) and a 'lion' (to frighten wolves); it is safer to be feared than loved if one cannot be both. He saw religion as useful for maintaining social order and unity (praising Roman religion), but criticised the Church for keeping Italy divided. 'Machiavellian' came to mean cunning and unscrupulous, but scholars note his realism and his patriotism (desire for a united Italy) and republicanism.
Machiavelli emphasises effective political leadership, preservation of the state and realistic analysis of power.

Machiavelli emphasised that the state's survival and power are the supreme goals. A strong state requires 'virtù' (the ability, energy and skill of the ruler to master circumstances) and luck ('fortuna'), which he compared to a river in flood - virtù builds dikes against it. He stressed that a state needs 'good laws and good arms', preferring a citizen army to mercenaries, whom he considered useless and dangerous.

He held a realistic view of human nature: people are 'ungrateful, fickle, liars and deceivers, fearful of danger and greedy for gain', so the ruler must use fear and force when necessary. He studied how principalities are acquired (by arms, fortune, crime or the favour of citizens) and maintained. In the 'Discourses', he praised the mixed constitution of the Roman Republic and the participation of citizens, showing that he valued liberty and republican government. He laid the foundation of the modern secular nation-state and of the concept of 'reason of state' (raison d'état).
Hobbes argues that individuals leave a dangerous state of nature by authorising a powerful sovereign to provide peace and security.

Thomas Hobbes (1588-1679) wrote 'Leviathan' (1651) during the period of the English Civil War. He described the state of nature as a condition without government, in which people are equal in their ability to kill each other and driven by self-interest, fear and the desire for power. It is a 'war of all against all' in which life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'. There is no justice, property or industry.

To escape this, people make a social contract with each other, agreeing to surrender all their rights (except the right of self-preservation) to a sovereign - one person or an assembly - who is not party to the contract. The sovereign is absolute, indivisible and unlimited; subjects cannot rebel (except if the sovereign threatens their lives), and the sovereign's laws define justice. The state, which he called the 'Leviathan' or 'mortal God', provides peace and security. Hobbes was the first to base the state on individual consent rather than divine right, but his conclusion supported absolutism. Critics note that his view of human nature is pessimistic and that his theory gives no protection against tyranny.
Locke sees political society as based on consent and created to protect natural rights, especially life, liberty and property.

John Locke (1632-1704) wrote 'Two Treatises of Government' (1690), justifying the Glorious Revolution of 1688. He described the state of nature as a state of peace, goodwill and mutual assistance, governed by natural law (reason) under which people have natural rights to life, liberty and property ('estate'). However, it has inconveniences: there is no established law, no impartial judge and no power to enforce decisions.

So people make a social contract, giving up only the right to interpret and enforce natural law, to establish a civil society and a limited government that protects their rights. Government is based on consent (including tacit consent), the majority rules, and the legislature is supreme but limited by natural law. If the government violates the trust by violating rights, the people have the right to resist and replace it (right of revolution). Locke also argued that property arises when a person mixes their labour with nature, and he supported religious toleration ('A Letter Concerning Toleration', 1689). He is the 'father of liberalism', influencing the American Declaration of Independence and constitutional democracy.
Rousseau argues that legitimate political authority must express the general will and that citizens should obey laws they prescribe collectively.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712-1778) wrote 'Discourse on the Origin of Inequality' (1755) and 'The Social Contract' (1762), which begins: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' The state of nature was idyllic - the 'noble savage' lived in simple happiness, guided by self-love (amour de soi) and pity. Private property, civilisation and society corrupted people, creating inequality, vanity (amour-propre) and conflict.

The social contract: each person gives himself entirely to the community, placing himself under the supreme direction of the 'general will'; in return, each becomes an indivisible part of the whole. The general will is the will of the community aimed at the common good, different from the 'will of all' (the sum of private interests). Sovereignty belongs to the people and is inalienable, indivisible and infallible; it cannot be represented, so Rousseau favoured direct democracy. Obedience to the general will is true freedom ('whoever refuses to obey the general will shall be forced to be free'). He is the 'father of popular sovereignty' and inspired the French Revolution. Critics (Benjamin Constant, J. L. Talmon - 'totalitarian democracy') argue that the general will can justify tyranny, while others see him as a theorist of radical democracy and equality.
Bentham's utilitarianism judges actions and institutions according to their tendency to promote the greatest happiness.

Jeremy Bentham (1748-1832), an English philosopher and legal reformer, wrote 'A Fragment on Government' (1776) and 'An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation' (1789). He began: 'Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure.' The principle of utility says that the right action is that which produces 'the greatest happiness of the greatest number'.

He proposed a 'felicific calculus' to measure pleasure and pain by intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity (nearness), fecundity, purity and extent. Bentham said 'quantity of pleasure being equal, pushpin is as good as poetry' - he made no distinction between higher and lower pleasures. He rejected natural rights ('nonsense upon stilts') and the social contract as fictions. He advocated legal and political reforms: codification of law, prison reform (the 'Panopticon' design), extension of suffrage, secret ballot, annual parliaments and a minimal but active state. Criticisms: pleasures cannot be measured; utilitarianism can justify sacrificing minorities; and it ignores rights and justice.
Mill strongly defends individual liberty and argues that coercion is justified mainly to prevent harm to others.

John Stuart Mill (1806-1873), son of James Mill and disciple of Bentham, revised utilitarianism by distinguishing higher (intellectual, moral) and lower (bodily) pleasures: 'It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.' In 'On Liberty' (1859), he defended the liberty of thought and expression, individuality and the 'harm principle': 'the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others.' His own good is not a sufficient reason.

He distinguished self-regarding actions (which concern only the individual and should be free) from other-regarding actions (which affect others and may be regulated). He defended freedom of speech because (1) the suppressed opinion may be true; (2) even if false, it may contain part of the truth; (3) truth unchallenged becomes 'dead dogma'; and (4) debate strengthens understanding. He warned against the 'tyranny of the majority' and social conformity. Criticisms: the distinction between self-regarding and other-regarding actions is difficult to draw, and his liberty was not for 'backward' societies, reflecting colonial attitudes (he worked for the East India Company).
Mill supports representative government while stressing political education, participation and protection against majority domination.

In 'Considerations on Representative Government' (1861), Mill argued that the ideally best form of government is representative government, because it protects people's interests and develops their intellectual and moral qualities through participation. He supported extending the franchise to all adults, including women ('The Subjection of Women', 1869), and as an MP (1865-1868) he proposed an amendment for women's suffrage.

However, to protect against the tyranny of the majority and the ignorance of the masses, he proposed: plural voting (more votes for the educated); excluding those who could not read, write and do basic arithmetic or who received poor relief; proportional representation (Thomas Hare's system) to protect minorities; open rather than secret ballot (to encourage public responsibility); a strong second chamber; and a legislative commission of experts to draft laws. Mill is regarded as a bridge between classical and modern liberalism, though his proposals for plural voting are considered elitist.
Hegel's dialectical method understands development through contradictions and their transformation within a larger historical process.

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel (1770-1831), a German idealist philosopher, wrote 'Phenomenology of Spirit' (1807) and 'Philosophy of Right' (1821). His dialectical method, often explained (though he did not use these exact terms) as thesis, antithesis and synthesis: every idea or situation (thesis) contains contradictions that give rise to its opposite (antithesis), and the conflict is resolved in a higher stage (synthesis), which becomes a new thesis. Change is thus progressive.

For Hegel, history is the progress of the 'Absolute Spirit' (Geist) or Reason realising itself, and the development of the consciousness of freedom: in the Oriental world, one person (the despot) was free; in the Greek and Roman world, some were free; and in the Germanic-Christian world, all are free. 'What is rational is actual and what is actual is rational.' His idealist dialectics influenced Marx, who 'turned Hegel upside down' by replacing ideas with matter.
Hegel regards the state as an important ethical institution in which individual and universal interests can be reconciled.

Hegel saw ethical life (Sittlichkeit) as developing through three stages: the family (based on love and unity - thesis), civil society (based on individual self-interest, competition, the market and needs - antithesis) and the state (synthesis), which reconciles particular interests with the universal good. The state is 'the march of God on earth', 'the actuality of the ethical idea' and 'the realisation of freedom'. Individuals find true freedom by identifying with the rational state.

He favoured a constitutional monarchy with a bureaucracy (the 'universal class') and representation of estates. He saw war as sometimes necessary to maintain the health of nations. Critics (Karl Popper, Bertrand Russell) argued that Hegel glorified the state and influenced totalitarianism (fascism), while defenders (Shlomo Avineri, Charles Taylor) see him as a theorist of a rational, constitutional state. He influenced both the right (state worship) and the left (Marx and the Young Hegelians).
Marxist dialectical materialism explains social development through material conditions and contradictions rather than primarily through ideas.

Dialectical materialism (a term used by later Marxists, especially Plekhanov and Engels) combines Hegel's dialectical method with materialism (Feuerbach): matter, not mind or ideas, is the primary reality; consciousness and ideas reflect material conditions. Marx said, 'It is not the consciousness of men that determines their being, but, on the contrary, their social being that determines their consciousness.'

Engels ('Dialectics of Nature', 'Anti-Dühring') stated three laws of dialectics: (1) the unity and struggle of opposites (contradictions within things cause change); (2) the transformation of quantity into quality (gradual changes lead to sudden qualitative change, like water becoming steam); and (3) the negation of the negation (development occurs in a spiral, preserving elements of earlier stages). Marx thus stood Hegel 'on his feet'. Critics argue that the laws are vague and cannot be scientifically tested (Popper).
Historical materialism interprets historical development through modes of production, economic relations and class structures.

Historical materialism applies dialectical materialism to society and history. In the Preface to 'A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy' (1859), Marx explained that the economic structure or 'base' - consisting of the forces of production (tools, technology, labour) and relations of production (ownership and class relations) - determines the 'superstructure' of law, politics, religion, art and philosophy.

History passes through stages based on modes of production: primitive communism (no private property, no classes), slavery (masters and slaves), feudalism (lords and serfs), capitalism (bourgeoisie and proletariat), and the future socialism and communism. Change occurs when the forces of production come into conflict with the relations of production, leading to class struggle and revolution. Criticisms: economic determinism ignores the independent role of ideas, religion, culture and individuals (Max Weber's 'Protestant Ethic' argued that ideas influenced capitalism); history has not followed the predicted stages; and later Marxists (Gramsci, Althusser) gave more importance to the superstructure.
Marx connects social revolution with contradictions in class society and transformation of the economic and political order.

Marx argued that revolution occurs when the contradictions between the forces and relations of production become acute. Under capitalism, contradictions include the concentration of wealth in fewer hands, the impoverishment and growing numbers of workers (the 'immiseration' of the proletariat), recurring economic crises of overproduction and the alienation of workers. Workers would develop class consciousness, from a 'class in itself' to a 'class for itself', organise and overthrow capitalism through revolution, possibly violent ('Workers of the world, unite! You have nothing to lose but your chains').

After the revolution, the 'dictatorship of the proletariat' would abolish private property in the means of production and suppress the bourgeoisie. This socialist stage ('from each according to his ability, to each according to his work') would lead to communism, a classless, stateless society ('from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs'), in which the state would 'wither away' (Engels). Marx expected revolution in advanced capitalist countries like England and Germany, but it happened in less developed Russia (1917) and China (1949), which Lenin and Mao explained through their own theories.
Marx sees class struggle between groups with opposed economic interests as a major force of historical change.

'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles' (Communist Manifesto, 1848). Classes are defined by their relation to the means of production: owners and non-owners. In each era, an exploiting class confronts an exploited class - freeman and slave, patrician and plebeian, lord and serf, guild-master and journeyman, and in capitalism, the bourgeoisie and the proletariat. Class interests are opposed and irreconcilable.

Capitalism simplifies class antagonisms into two great classes, as the middle classes (small producers, artisans) sink into the proletariat. The state, law and ideology serve the ruling class ('the ideas of the ruling class are in every epoch the ruling ideas'). Class struggle ends only with the abolition of classes under communism. Criticisms: modern societies have a large middle class, the welfare state and trade unions have improved workers' conditions, and other identities (nation, religion, race, gender) often matter more than class. Max Weber argued that stratification involves class, status and party.
Surplus value refers to the value produced by labour beyond what workers receive in wages and is central to Marx's analysis of capitalist exploitation.

In 'Capital' (Das Kapital, Volume I, 1867), Marx developed the labour theory of value (from Adam Smith and David Ricardo): the value of a commodity is determined by the socially necessary labour time required to produce it. Labour power is a special commodity because it can produce more value than its own value (the cost of the worker's subsistence). The capitalist buys labour power for wages equal to its value, but makes the worker work longer than needed to produce that value.

For example, if a worker produces the value of his daily wage in six hours but works twelve, the value produced in the extra six hours is 'surplus value', appropriated by the capitalist as profit. This is the source of exploitation. Capitalists increase surplus value by lengthening the working day (absolute surplus value) or increasing productivity through machinery (relative surplus value). Marx predicted that competition and mechanisation would lead to a falling rate of profit and crises. Critics (Böhm-Bawerk, marginalist economists) argue that value depends on utility and demand, and that capital, risk and entrepreneurship also create value.

sections.title: Plato: Justice, Education, Communism and Ideal State

blocks.text:
Plato's political thought is closely connected with his search for justice. He views justice as harmony in which each part of society performs its proper function. His ideal state is divided into functional classes and governed by philosopher-rulers.

Education is essential because it develops character and helps identify those capable of governing. Plato also proposes communal arrangements for the guardian class so that private property and family interests do not distract them from public duty.

His theory is highly influential, although many features of the ideal state conflict with modern democratic ideas.

Plato's theory of justice: rejecting conventional views (Cephalus, Polemarchus, Thrasymachus, Glaucon), Plato defined justice as each class performing its proper function - rulers (reason, wisdom), auxiliaries (spirit, courage) and producers (appetite, temperance) - in harmony. Justice is the principle of specialisation and non-interference, both in the soul and the state. It is a moral and functional concept rather than legal.

Education and communism: state-controlled education for men and women, from music and gymnastics to mathematics and dialectics, selects and trains philosopher-rulers; communism of property and family for the guardian classes prevents corruption and promotes unity. Ideal state: rule of philosopher-kings who know the 'Form of the Good', three classes based on aptitude (myth of metals), equality of women, and rule by knowledge rather than law.

Evaluation: Plato's contributions include the idea that rulers must be qualified and devoted to the public good, the importance of education, equality of women (revolutionary for his time) and the search for a just society. Criticisms: authoritarianism (Popper), neglect of individual liberty and consent, rigid class division, censorship, lack of checks on rulers, utopianism and the exclusion of producers from political life. In 'The Laws', Plato himself moved towards a more practical state based on law. His work remains foundational to Western political philosophy.

sections.title: Aristotle: Constitutions, Best State, Revolution and Slavery

blocks.text:
Aristotle studies political institutions in a more empirical and comparative manner. He classifies constitutions according to who rules and whether rule serves the common interest or private interest.

Rather than seeking only an ideal state, he discusses the best practicable constitution and values moderation. He analyses inequality and injustice as important causes of revolution.

Aristotle also defended natural slavery, an argument that is incompatible with modern ideas of human equality and rights.

Aristotle's method was empirical and comparative, based on the study of 158 constitutions; he is called the father of Political Science. Man is a 'political animal', and the state (polis) exists 'for the sake of the good life'. Classification of constitutions: by number of rulers and purpose - monarchy/tyranny, aristocracy/oligarchy, polity/democracy - with a cycle of change. Best practicable state: polity, a mixed constitution with a large middle class and the golden mean, rule of law and moderate citizenship qualifications.

Revolution: caused by disputes over justice and inequality (the many want equality, the few want superiority), and particular causes such as insolence, fear, contempt, disproportionate growth of classes and neglect of small changes; prevented by rule of law, moderation, strong middle class, education in the constitution and honest administration. Slavery: Aristotle defended natural slavery - some are by nature rulers and others slaves - while recommending humane treatment; he also considered women inferior to men and denied citizenship to labourers.

Evaluation: Aristotle's realism, empiricism and emphasis on the middle class, rule of law and mixed constitution influenced later thinkers (Polybius, Aquinas, Montesquieu, the US founders). His views on slavery and women reflect the prejudices of his society and are rejected by modern principles of equality. Comparing Plato and Aristotle: Plato was idealist, deductive and favoured rule by philosophers; Aristotle was realist, inductive and favoured rule of law and a practical constitution - Raphael's painting 'The School of Athens' shows Plato pointing upward and Aristotle pointing to the earth.

Machiavelli is known for treating politics as an autonomous field of practical activity. He studies how rulers acquire, preserve and use power and gives priority to the security and stability of the state.

Religion and morality are examined partly in terms of their political effects. His analysis does not simply ask what a morally perfect ruler should do; it asks what political leadership requires under difficult real conditions.

This realistic approach is one reason Machiavelli is often regarded as an important figure in the development of modern political thought.

Background: Renaissance Italy was divided into city-states and principalities, often controlled by foreign powers (France, Spain) and the Papacy. Machiavelli, a patriot, wanted a strong ruler to unify Italy and expel foreigners (the last chapter of The Prince is an 'Exhortation to liberate Italy from the barbarians'). He used historical examples (ancient Rome, Cesare Borgia) and observation rather than abstract principles.

Separation of politics from ethics and religion: the ruler should follow 'reason of state' - doing whatever is necessary to preserve the state, even if immoral (deception, cruelty used wisely). He distinguished private morality from public morality; a ruler should appear virtuous but be willing to act otherwise. Religion is useful as a tool for unity and obedience, but the Church had corrupted Italy. Human nature is selfish, so rulers must use fear; 'virtù' and 'fortuna'; good laws and good arms (a citizen militia).

Evaluation: Machiavelli is the father of modern political science and realism because he described politics as it is, not as it should be. He contributed to the concept of the secular sovereign state and nationalism. Critics condemned him as immoral ('Old Nick'); defenders (Isaiah Berlin) argue that he recognised the conflict between different moral systems - Christian virtue and civic virtue. His 'Discourses' show his admiration for republican liberty and citizen participation.

sections.title: Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau: Social Contract

blocks.text:
Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau all use the idea of a social contract but reach different conclusions. Hobbes describes the state of nature as insecure and supports a powerful sovereign to maintain peace.

Locke argues that individuals possess natural rights and create limited government through consent to protect life, liberty and property. Rousseau places emphasis on popular sovereignty and the general will.

Their theories helped shape modern debates about authority, consent, rights and democratic legitimacy.

Hobbes ('Leviathan', 1651): pessimistic view of human nature (selfish, fearful, power-seeking); state of nature as war of all against all ('nasty, brutish and short'); contract among individuals to surrender all rights to an absolute sovereign who is not a party to the contract; sovereign's power is unlimited and indivisible; no right of rebellion except self-preservation. Contribution: the state is based on consent and created for security; individualism; legal sovereignty. Criticism: absolutism, pessimism.

Locke ('Two Treatises', 1690): human nature is rational and sociable; the state of nature is peaceful, governed by natural law, with natural rights to life, liberty and property, but with inconveniences; the contract creates a limited government based on consent and trust; government protects natural rights; the legislature is supreme but limited; and people have a right to resist and change a government that violates their rights. Contribution: liberalism, constitutionalism, limited government, popular consent and the right of revolution. Criticism: defence of property can justify inequality; tacit consent is vague.

Rousseau ('The Social Contract', 1762): man is naturally good, corrupted by society and property; the contract involves total alienation of each to the community, creating a collective body guided by the general will; sovereignty belongs to the people, is inalienable and indivisible, and cannot be represented; true freedom is obedience to self-prescribed law. Contribution: popular sovereignty, democracy and equality; inspiration for the French Revolution. Criticism: the general will is vague and may justify tyranny. Comparison: Hobbes leads to absolute monarchy, Locke to limited constitutional government, and Rousseau to popular sovereignty and direct democracy.

Bentham develops utilitarianism around the principle of promoting the greatest happiness. Laws and institutions should therefore be judged by their consequences for human welfare.

J.S. Mill also works within the utilitarian tradition but gives strong protection to individuality and liberty. His harm principle limits coercion mainly to preventing harm to others. Mill also supports representative government and values political participation.

Together Bentham and Mill are major contributors to liberal and utilitarian political thought.

Bentham: the principle of utility ('greatest happiness of the greatest number'); human behaviour governed by pleasure and pain; felicific calculus; no qualitative distinction between pleasures; rejection of natural rights and the social contract; law as the command of the sovereign; reforms - codification, prison reform (Panopticon), democratic reforms (extension of suffrage, secret ballot), and a state that promotes happiness through legislation. Criticisms: pleasures cannot be measured; majority happiness may sacrifice minorities; it ignores justice and rights.

J. S. Mill: qualitative utilitarianism (higher and lower pleasures); 'On Liberty' (1859) - harm principle, freedom of thought and expression, individuality and the danger of social tyranny; representative government as the best form ('Considerations on Representative Government', 1861), with universal suffrage including women, but plural voting for the educated, proportional representation and safeguards against majority tyranny; 'The Subjection of Women' (1869) argued for gender equality. Mill moved from classical to modern liberalism, recognising a role for the state in education and labour.

Evaluation: Bentham and Mill shaped liberal and utilitarian thought, legal reform and democratic institutions in Britain and beyond, including India (Bentham's influence on codification - the Indian Penal Code of 1860, drafted by Macaulay, reflects utilitarian ideas; Mill worked for the East India Company). Mill's defence of liberty remains central to debates on free speech, while his elitism and colonial views are criticised.

Hegel understands historical and intellectual development through dialectical processes involving contradiction and transformation. Political institutions develop within this broader historical movement.

For Hegel, the state is not merely an instrument of coercion. It is an ethical institution through which individual and universal interests can be reconciled.

His theory greatly influenced later political thought, including thinkers who adopted or criticised his dialectical method.

Hegel's dialectics: reality and history develop through contradictions - thesis, antithesis and synthesis - as the 'World Spirit' (Geist) realises itself and achieves self-consciousness and freedom. History is the progress of freedom: from one free (Oriental despotism) to some free (Greek and Roman) to all free (the Germanic-Christian world). 'The owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of the dusk' - philosophy understands an era only when it is ending.

Theory of the state: ethical life develops through the family (unity based on love), civil society (the system of needs, market, competition, administration of justice and corporations) and the state (the synthesis, in which the universal and particular are reconciled). The state is the 'actuality of the ethical idea', 'the march of God on earth', an end in itself rather than a means for individuals. Hegel favoured constitutional monarchy, bureaucracy as the universal class and representation through estates.

Evaluation: Hegel contributed the dialectical method, a historical understanding of institutions and the idea of the state as an ethical community. Critics such as Popper and Russell said his glorification of the state led to authoritarianism and nationalism (German and Italian fascism), and Marx criticised his idealism. Others argue that Hegel's state is a constitutional, rational one protecting freedom. His influence extends to Marxism, existentialism, critical theory and communitarianism.

sections.title: Marx: Materialism, Revolution, Class Struggle and Surplus Value

blocks.text:
Marx transforms dialectical analysis by emphasising material and economic conditions. Historical materialism explains social change through modes of production and class relations.

Class struggle is a central force of history because social classes may have opposed economic interests. Marx connects capitalist society with exploitation and explains surplus value as value created by labour beyond what workers receive as wages.

Contradictions within class society can produce revolutionary change and transformation of the political and economic order.

Dialectical and historical materialism: Marx combined Hegel's dialectics with materialism; the economic base (forces and relations of production) determines the superstructure (law, politics, ideology); history moves through modes of production - primitive communism, slavery, feudalism, capitalism, socialism and communism - driven by contradictions between forces and relations of production. Class struggle: history is a history of class struggles; in capitalism, between the bourgeoisie and the proletariat; the state is an instrument of class domination.

Surplus value and exploitation: according to the labour theory of value, workers produce more value than they receive as wages; the difference (surplus value) is appropriated by capitalists as profit, which is the basis of exploitation. Capitalism also produces alienation of workers from their product, labour, fellow workers and their human essence ('Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts', 1844). Revolution: capitalist contradictions (crises, concentration of capital, growing proletariat and class consciousness) lead to a proletarian revolution, the dictatorship of the proletariat, socialism and finally a classless, stateless communist society.

Evaluation: Marx's analysis of capitalism, class, exploitation and ideology has deeply influenced social science and political movements (Russian, Chinese, Cuban and Vietnamese revolutions; socialist and labour parties; the welfare state). Criticisms: economic determinism; predictions of proletarian revolution in advanced capitalist countries failed; capitalism adapted through reforms; communist states became authoritarian; the labour theory of value is disputed; and the neglect of nationalism, religion, gender and individual rights. Neo-Marxists (Gramsci, the Frankfurt School, Althusser) revised Marx's ideas, and his critique remains relevant in debates on inequality and globalisation.
International organisation refers to organised cooperation among states through institutions created to address common international concerns.

International organisations are formal institutions created by agreement among states (intergovernmental organisations, IGOs - such as the UN, WTO, IMF, ASEAN, SAARC, African Union, NATO) or by private actors (international NGOs - such as Amnesty International, the International Committee of the Red Cross, Greenpeace). IGOs have a permanent structure, members, rules and functions. Early examples include the Concert of Europe (1815), international river commissions (the Rhine, 1815), the International Telegraph Union (1865) and the Universal Postal Union (1874). The League of Nations (1920) was the first general political organisation.

Functions: providing a forum for negotiation, making rules and norms, maintaining peace and security, promoting economic and social cooperation, providing services (health, development aid) and monitoring compliance. Theories: realists see international organisations as tools of powerful states; liberal institutionalists see them as facilitating cooperation by reducing transaction costs and building trust; constructivists see them as shaping norms and identities; and functionalists (David Mitrany, 'A Working Peace System', 1943) see technical cooperation leading to peace.
The UN was established after the Second World War as an international organisation intended to promote peace, security and cooperation.

Steps leading to the UN: the London Declaration (June 1941); the Atlantic Charter (14 August 1941) of Roosevelt and Churchill; the Declaration by United Nations (1 January 1942), signed by 26 nations fighting the Axis (the name 'United Nations' was coined by Roosevelt); the Moscow Declaration (October 1943) calling for a general international organisation; the Tehran Conference (1943); the Dumbarton Oaks Conference (August-October 1944) in Washington, where the USA, UK, USSR and China drafted proposals; and the Yalta Conference (February 1945), which agreed on Security Council voting (the veto).

The United Nations Conference on International Organization (San Francisco, 25 April - 26 June 1945) was attended by 50 countries, which signed the Charter on 26 June 1945 (Poland signed later as the 51st original member). The UN came into existence on 24 October 1945 (UN Day) after ratification by the five permanent members and a majority of signatories. India was a founding member, signing the Charter in 1945 even before independence. The UN headquarters is in New York (land donated by John D. Rockefeller Jr.); other offices are in Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi. The UN replaced the League of Nations, which was formally dissolved in 1946.
The UN Charter is the founding document of the United Nations and establishes its purposes, principles, organs and legal framework.

The UN Charter has a Preamble and 111 articles in 19 chapters. The Preamble begins: 'We the peoples of the United Nations determined to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war, which twice in our lifetime has brought untold sorrow to mankind, and to reaffirm faith in fundamental human rights, in the dignity and worth of the human person, in the equal rights of men and women and of nations large and small...'

Important chapters: I (Purposes and Principles), III (Organs), IV-V (General Assembly and Security Council), VI (Pacific Settlement of Disputes), VII (Action with respect to Threats to the Peace, Breaches of the Peace and Acts of Aggression - enforcement measures, Articles 39-51, including Article 51 on the right of self-defence), VIII (Regional Arrangements), IX-X (International Economic and Social Cooperation, ECOSOC), XI-XIII (Non-Self-Governing Territories and Trusteeship), XIV (International Court of Justice) and XV (Secretariat). Article 103 makes Charter obligations prevail over other treaties. Amendment (Article 108) requires a two-thirds vote of the General Assembly and ratification by two-thirds of members, including all five permanent members. The Charter has been amended a few times (enlarging the Security Council from 11 to 15 in 1965 and ECOSOC from 18 to 27 and then 54).
Major objectives include maintaining international peace and security, developing friendly relations and promoting international cooperation.

Article 1 lists the purposes: (1) to maintain international peace and security, taking effective collective measures to prevent and remove threats to peace and suppress acts of aggression, and to settle disputes by peaceful means in conformity with justice and international law; (2) to develop friendly relations among nations based on respect for the principle of equal rights and self-determination of peoples; (3) to achieve international cooperation in solving international problems of an economic, social, cultural or humanitarian character, and in promoting respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms for all without distinction as to race, sex, language or religion; and (4) to be a centre for harmonising the actions of nations in attaining these common ends.

These objectives have expanded in practice to include peacekeeping, decolonisation, development (the Millennium Development Goals, 2000-2015, and the Sustainable Development Goals, 2015-2030, with 17 goals), environmental protection (climate change conferences under the UNFCCC, the Paris Agreement 2015), humanitarian assistance, disarmament and counter-terrorism.
The Charter includes principles such as sovereign equality of members, peaceful settlement of disputes and fulfilment of Charter obligations.

Article 2 lists seven principles: (1) sovereign equality of all members; (2) members shall fulfil in good faith the obligations of the Charter; (3) members shall settle their disputes by peaceful means; (4) members shall refrain from the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state; (5) members shall give the UN every assistance in any action it takes and refrain from assisting any state against which the UN is taking preventive or enforcement action; (6) the UN shall ensure that non-member states act in accordance with these principles as necessary for peace; and (7) the UN shall not intervene in matters essentially within the domestic jurisdiction of any state, except for enforcement measures under Chapter VII.

These principles reflect the Westphalian ideas of sovereignty and non-intervention, combined with collective security. Tensions have arisen between non-intervention and the protection of human rights, leading to debates on humanitarian intervention and the 'Responsibility to Protect' (2005). Violations, such as the US-led invasion of Iraq (2003) and Russia's invasion of Ukraine (2022), have raised questions about the UN's effectiveness.
The General Assembly is the main deliberative body in which all UN member states are represented.

The General Assembly (Chapter IV, Articles 9-22) consists of all 193 member states, each with one vote (sovereign equality). It meets in regular annual sessions from September (the 'general debate' of world leaders) and in special and emergency special sessions. It elects a President each year (Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit of India was the first woman President of the General Assembly, 1953). Decisions on important questions (peace and security, admission of members, budget, elections to councils) require a two-thirds majority; other questions a simple majority.

Functions: deliberative (it can discuss any matter within the scope of the Charter and make recommendations - except on disputes being dealt with by the Security Council, Article 12); financial (approves the UN budget and members' contributions); elective (elects the non-permanent members of the Security Council, members of ECOSOC and, with the Security Council, judges of the ICJ; appoints the Secretary-General on the Council's recommendation; admits new members on the Council's recommendation); and constituent (participates in Charter amendments). The 'Uniting for Peace' Resolution (1950) allows the General Assembly to recommend collective action when the Security Council is deadlocked by the veto. Its resolutions are not legally binding (except on internal matters), but carry moral weight; it has been called 'the town meeting of the world'.
The Security Council has primary responsibility under the Charter for international peace and security.

The Security Council (Chapter V, Articles 23-32) has 15 members: five permanent members (P5) - China, France, Russia (successor to the USSR since 1991), the United Kingdom and the United States - and ten non-permanent members elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms (five each year) on a regional basis; they cannot be immediately re-elected. India has been a non-permanent member eight times, most recently in 2021-2022. The presidency rotates monthly.

Voting (Article 27): procedural matters require nine affirmative votes; substantive matters require nine votes including the concurring votes of all permanent members - this is the 'veto' (abstention by a permanent member is not considered a veto by practice). The Soviet Union/Russia and the USA have used the veto most often. Powers: investigating disputes, recommending methods of settlement (Chapter VI), determining threats to peace and deciding on enforcement measures - economic sanctions, arms embargoes, and military action (Chapter VII, Articles 41-42), establishing peacekeeping operations, recommending admission of members and the appointment of the Secretary-General, and electing ICJ judges with the General Assembly. Its decisions are binding on all members (Article 25).
ECOSOC coordinates and promotes international economic, social and related cooperation.

ECOSOC (Chapter X, Articles 61-72) has 54 members elected by the General Assembly for three-year terms (18 each year), with regional distribution. It coordinates the economic, social, humanitarian and environmental work of the UN, its specialised agencies, funds and programmes, and functional and regional commissions (such as the Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific, ESCAP, in Bangkok, and the Commission on the Status of Women).

Functions: making studies and reports on international economic, social, cultural, educational and health matters; making recommendations to the General Assembly, members and specialised agencies; promoting respect for human rights; preparing draft conventions; calling international conferences; coordinating specialised agencies through agreements; and consulting with NGOs (over 5,000 NGOs have consultative status). It holds the High-Level Political Forum on Sustainable Development, which reviews progress on the SDGs. Critics say it is too large and has limited influence compared with institutions like the IMF and World Bank.
The Secretariat carries out the administrative work of the UN under the leadership of the Secretary-General.

The Secretariat (Chapter XV, Articles 97-101) is the administrative organ, with about 37,000 international civil servants worldwide, who must be independent and not take instructions from any government (Article 100). It is headed by the Secretary-General, appointed by the General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council (subject to veto) for a five-year term, renewable once by convention.

The Secretary-General is the 'chief administrative officer' (Article 97), attends meetings of the main organs, presents the annual report, may bring to the Security Council's attention any matter that threatens peace (Article 99), uses 'good offices' for mediation, and acts as the UN's spokesperson. Secretaries-General: Trygve Lie (Norway, 1946-1952), Dag Hammarskjöld (Sweden, 1953-1961, died in a plane crash in Congo, posthumous Nobel Peace Prize), U Thant (Burma, 1961-1971), Kurt Waldheim (Austria), Javier Pérez de Cuéllar (Peru), Boutros Boutros-Ghali (Egypt, 'An Agenda for Peace', 1992), Kofi Annan (Ghana, 1997-2006, Nobel Peace Prize 2001), Ban Ki-moon (South Korea, 2007-2016) and António Guterres (Portugal, since 2017). No woman has yet held the post.
The ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the UN and settles legal disputes between states that fall within its jurisdiction and gives advisory opinions.

The International Court of Justice (Chapter XIV and the ICJ Statute), located at the Peace Palace in The Hague, Netherlands, succeeded the Permanent Court of International Justice of the League. It has 15 judges elected for nine-year terms by absolute majorities in both the General Assembly and the Security Council, with no two judges from the same country; one-third are elected every three years. Indian judges have included B. N. Rau, Nagendra Singh (President, 1985-1988), R. S. Pathak and Dalveer Bhandari (since 2012).

Jurisdiction: contentious cases between states that consent to its jurisdiction (by special agreement, treaty clauses or optional declarations under Article 36(2)); only states can be parties. Its judgements are binding on the parties; if a party fails to comply, the other may approach the Security Council (Article 94). Advisory opinions are given on legal questions referred by UN organs and agencies (for example, on the legality of nuclear weapons, 1996, the Israeli wall, 2004, Kosovo's declaration of independence, 2010, and Israel's occupation of Palestinian territories, 2024). India's cases include the Kulbhushan Jadhav case against Pakistan (2017-2019), in which the ICJ ruled in India's favour on consular access. Limitations: consent-based jurisdiction and lack of enforcement.
The International Labour Organization promotes labour standards, decent work and social justice.

The ILO was established in 1919 under the Treaty of Versailles, became the first specialised agency of the UN in 1946, and is headquartered in Geneva. It has a unique tripartite structure: governments, employers and workers are represented in its General Conference (the International Labour Conference), the Governing Body and other organs. It won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1969. India is a founding member.

Functions: setting international labour standards through conventions and recommendations (about 190 conventions on freedom of association, forced labour, child labour - Conventions 138 and 182, discrimination, working hours, safety and social security); supervising their application; providing technical assistance; promoting the 'Decent Work Agenda' (employment, rights at work, social protection and social dialogue); research and statistics; and the Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work (1998), covering freedom of association, elimination of forced labour, abolition of child labour, elimination of discrimination and (since 2022) a safe and healthy working environment.
UNESCO works in education, science, culture and related areas of international cooperation.

UNESCO (United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization) was founded on 16 November 1945, with headquarters in Paris. Its constitution states: 'Since wars begin in the minds of men, it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be constructed.' It has about 194 member states (the USA has withdrawn and rejoined several times, most recently rejoining in 2023 and announcing withdrawal again in 2025).
